card.hook: Picture Smith Tower rising up behind a parking garage that everyone calls the sinking ship. Now picture it upside down in a puddle at your feet. That's the Pioneer Square shot.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of James Street and Yesler Way, near the parking garage known as the sinking ship. Face the garage so Smith Tower rises behind it. The small plaza and the pergola are a short walk to the east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the tower, the garage and the street all fit in one frame. Try 1x for a tighter, calmer shot. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it to pick out the top of the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the tower on one of the vertical lines, and keep your phone level so the tall building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Just after rain is best, when puddles have formed and can reflect the tower and the buildings. Hold your phone low over a puddle, tap the puddle, and let the reflection be the star.
card.selfie_here: Head to Pioneer Place Park, next to the iron pergola, and try a selfie with the totem pole in the frame. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you have it, and tuck the pergola in over your shoulder. Nobody's pinned down an exact selfie spot, so wander a bit and see what works.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the sidewalk at the corner of 1st Avenue and Yesler Way, while you stand with the pergola behind you, so they can fit the whole thing in.
card.rules_and_safety: Pioneer Square isn't always the safest place at night, so visit during the day, especially if you're on your own. Keep an eye on your phone and your surroundings while you frame your shots.
card.challenge: Find a puddle, get low, and make Smith Tower stand on its head. Bonus points if nobody's boots are in the shot.
card.good_to_know: Seattle's founders settled here in 1852. Most of the early wooden buildings burned in the Great Seattle Fire of 1889, and by the end of 1890 dozens of brick and stone buildings had replaced them. Those buildings, mostly Richardsonian Romanesque, still give the neighbourhood its look, and the area is a historic district on the National Register of Historic Places.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of James Street and Yesler Way, near the parking garage known as the sinking ship. Face the garage so Smith Tower rises behind it. The small plaza and the pergola are a short walk to the east.

card.hook: Picture a hilltop railing, a skyline, and one flying saucer on a stick sitting right in the middle of it. That's the Space Needle from Kerry Park, and it's the shot everyone comes up the hill for.
card.stand_here: Walk up Queen Anne hill to Kerry Park, which sits north-west of the tower, and stand at the south-facing overlook railing. Face out over downtown and the Needle should be right in the middle of the skyline, with Elliott Bay alongside.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole skyline, bay and Needle together. Then try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for a tighter shot with Mount Rainier behind. Zoom 0.5x makes the Needle look small, so save it for a scene-setting shot with the railing and sky.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the Needle on one of the vertical lines, then tap it and slide a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Sunset or blue hour gives the best light, and night mode can help once it gets dim (rest your phone on the railing to keep it steady). The park fills up before sunset, so arrive early. Mount Rainier only shows on clear days, so check the forecast before you climb the hill.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and hold it a bit low and out to the side, so the skyline fits behind you. Try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it on the front, and keep the Needle over your shoulder rather than behind your head.
card.rules_and_safety: Kerry Park is an open public park and free to enter. It's small and gets busy before sunset, and street parking can be hard to find, so walking up is often easier.
card.challenge: Get the Needle standing perfectly upright on a grid line, with a little sky above the saucer and Mount Rainier peeking out behind it.
card.good_to_know: The Space Needle was built for the 1962 World's Fair, which drew more than 2.3 million visitors. It stands 605 ft (184 m) tall, and when it was finished it was the tallest building west of the Mississippi River. Skyscrapers have since overtaken it, but it's still Seattle's best-known tower.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk up Queen Anne hill to Kerry Park, which sits north-west of the tower, and stand at the south-facing overlook railing. Face out over downtown and the Needle should be right in the middle of the skyline, with Elliott Bay alongside.

card.hook: Everyone clusters right under the big red neon sign, but the sign sits at the bottom of a slope, so the cleaner shot is from up the hill.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of 1st Avenue and Pine Street, in the centre of the crosswalk uphill from the sign. Face the red neon Public Market Center sign and clock, with the market entrance and street life behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the sign head-on. If crowds or traffic stop you stepping back, try zoom 0.5x for more street and sky, or zoom 2x to bring the sign closer without walking into the road.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the sign in the middle and line the clock up with a horizontal line, then tap the sign so it looks sharp.
card.best_time: Go early if you can, because it gets very busy at the sign. Take a few shots either way, since people and vehicles keep drifting through the frame.
card.selfie_here: Try the smaller Public Market sign at the end of Pine Street, one block over from the main entrance sign. Guides say you can shoot it from higher ground, which makes it easier to crop out other people. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and check the sign is over your shoulder before you tap.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to climb the steps toward Storyville Coffee in the Corner Market building (kitty-corner from the main sign corner) and shoot down at you while you pose on the brick street below.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos are fine for visitors. The crosswalk is an all-way crossing, so only step into the middle during the walk signal. One guide says once cars get a red light you have about 26 seconds to step in, shoot and get back to the curb, though guides differ slightly on the timing.
card.challenge: Get the neon sign, the clock and your grin all in one frame, with the clock sitting perfectly level on your gridline.
card.good_to_know: Pike Place Market opened on 17 August 1907 and is one of the older continuously operated public farmers' markets in the United States. More than 20 million people visit every year. It's built on a steep hill, with fish, fresh produce and crafts in the upper-level arcades and more shops on the levels below.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of 1st Avenue and Pine Street, in the centre of the crosswalk uphill from the sign. Face the red neon Public Market Center sign and clock, with the market entrance and street life behind it.

card.hook: Picture a brick wall dressed head to toe in chewing gum, every colour you can think of, and thousands of tiny details to hunt for. It's gross, it's glorious, and it makes a great backdrop.
card.stand_here: Stand right in front of the Gum Wall in Post Alley, beside the Market Theater box office. The phone icon on the map marks the wall itself. Face the bricks head-on so the gum fills the picture.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the head-on shot with you or a friend in front. If the alley is too tight to fit everything, switch to 0.5x. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for close-ups of a few bricks and little gum shapes.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the wall, then slide the brightness to darker if the brightest gum looks washed out.
card.best_time: Go early morning or late afternoon, when there are usually fewer people behind you. Summer afternoons and weekends are the busiest.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie at the wall beside the Market Theater box office, a spot couples and wedding photographers love. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if the alley feels tight, and keep the gum behind your shoulder. You can also come down the stairs to the left of the Pike Place Market sign into Post Alley, where the wall is on your left.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand a few steps back down Post Alley, far enough away to fit the whole run of wall, while you stand in front of the gum.
card.rules_and_safety: Please don't touch the wall, and don't let children or bags lean on it. There's gum on the ground too, so watch where you step.
card.challenge: Find a love message or a tiny gum artwork and make it the star of a close-up.
card.good_to_know: The Gum Wall began by accident in the 1990s, when people going to shows at the Market Theater started sticking gum to the wall. Market officials decided to let it stay, and it became a local landmark. It's about 54 feet (16 m) long and 8 feet (2.4 m) high as of 2024. It's been steam-cleaned several times, most recently in November 2024, so the amount of gum you see changes over time.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right in front of the Gum Wall in Post Alley, beside the Market Theater box office. The phone icon on the map marks the wall itself. Face the bricks head-on so the gum fills the picture.

card.hook: Imagine a tower of bright glass shooting up from the plants, with the Space Needle standing right behind it like the world's tallest photobomber. That's the Garden at Chihuly Garden and Glass.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, in the Garden at Chihuly Garden and Glass, right beside the Space Needle in Seattle Center. Face the Needle, with one of the tall glass towers in front of it.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for a glass tower with the Space Needle behind it. Go to 0.5x inside the Glasshouse to fit the huge sculpture overhead. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out one tower or one glass globe.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the glass tower, then slide it a little darker so the sky stays blue and the colours look rich (a bit more if the glass looks washed out).
card.best_time: Opening hours vary, so check before you go. Soft, low light like late afternoon usually makes the glass colours richer than harsh midday sun.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a little low. Turn so a bright glass sculpture sits over your shoulder, and take a few steps sideways between shots, because the background shifts.
card.ask_someone: Ask a member of staff or one of the roving photographers for a photo, or ask someone at the north end of the outdoor garden path, where the Space Needle looks best, and check the framing on the spot.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your phone about 12 inches (30 cm) from any glass, leave the flash off, and remember selfie sticks aren't allowed.
card.challenge: Crouch beside a big glass globe and catch the Space Needle's bent, coloured reflection inside it. Can you get it without your own face photobombing?
card.good_to_know: Chihuly Garden and Glass opened on 21 May 2012, on the site of the old Fun Forest amusement park. It has three main parts: the Garden, the Glasshouse and the indoor exhibits. The suspended sculpture in the Glasshouse is about 100 feet (around 30 metres) long and is one of Chihuly's largest. It's admission-only, so check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, in the Garden at Chihuly Garden and Glass, right beside the Space Needle in Seattle Center. Face the Needle, with one of the tall glass towers in front of it.

card.hook: Picture someone crumpled up a giant sheet of shiny, multicoloured metal and set it down next to the Space Needle. That's the Museum of Pop Culture, and your phone is going to love it.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Seattle Center grounds on the Space Needle side of the museum, with the building to the east of you. Face the shiny panels and you'll see the tower and the campus trees reflected in them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole building and the Space Needle in one frame. Switch to 1x for cleaner, less stretched views of the panels. If your phone has 2x to 5x, use it to fill the frame with panel colours and patterns.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest panel, then drag the brightness down a little so the colours don't wash out and the reflections stay visible.
card.best_time: A clear day gives the strongest reflections. Low sun at sunrise or sunset, or late afternoon, brings out the richest colours in the panels.
card.selfie_here: Try the roundabout in front of the building, with the silver exterior behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a bit higher so the curves fill the space over your shoulder. Check the spot when you arrive, as it's only loosely pinned down.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the outside from the open Seattle Center grounds without paying admission. Photo rules inside vary by exhibit, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find three spots where the same wall looks like a completely different colour, and take one shot from each.
card.good_to_know: Paul Allen founded the museum in 2000 as the Experience Music Project. It took the name Museum of Pop Culture in November 2016. Frank O. Gehry designed the building, which covers about 140,000 square feet (13,000 m²).
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Seattle Center grounds on the Space Needle side of the museum, with the building to the east of you. Face the shiny panels and you'll see the tower and the campus trees reflected in them.

card.hook: Here's a handy trick: don't stand at the aquarium to photograph it. Walk out onto a pier, turn around, and the aquarium, the water, the skyline and the Great Wheel all squeeze into one picture.
card.stand_here: Stand at the north end of Pier 62, just north-west of the aquarium. Face back across the water and the Pier 59 building is to the south-east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the aquarium, skyline and Great Wheel all in. Then try 1x for a cleaner look at the building, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick the aquarium out from across the water.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the aquarium building, then drag the brightness slider down a touch if the sky is bright, so the building and water keep their detail.
card.best_time: Try the afternoon or early evening, which our notes say should light up the aquarium side of the view. Take a quick test shot when you arrive to check how the light looks.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the Pier 62 dock, facing back toward the aquarium next door. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and tuck the aquarium over your shoulder. Check the screen to make sure it's in the frame.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from a few steps back while you stand on the pier next to the Aquarium Pavilion, so the Great Wheel shows up behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the aquarium's website before you go for tickets, opening times and any waterfront closures or construction.
card.challenge: Get the aquarium, the Great Wheel and a strip of water in one shot, with the pier edge dead straight. Bonus points if you keep it level on the first try.
card.good_to_know: The Seattle Aquarium opened on 20 May 1977, with its original buildings on Pier 59 and Pier 60. The newer Ocean Pavilion opened in August 2024. Its yellow cedar outside is designed to look like driftwood, with artwork by Lummi artist Dan Friday.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the north end of Pier 62, just north-west of the aquarium. Face back across the water and the Pier 59 building is to the south-east.

card.hook: T-Mobile Park is so big that standing right next to it, you'll struggle to get it all in your phone. So do what the locals' postcards do and step back and up.
card.stand_here: Stand in Dr. Jose Rizal Park, on the Beacon Hill hillside east of the stadium, and face the ballpark so you're looking down over it. The map will route you there, and the Navigate buttons take you to the subject.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to catch the city, Puget Sound and the Olympic Mountains. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the ballpark closer. Skip 0.5x here, because it shrinks the stadium to a speck.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the stadium on the lower third line, with the skyline, water and mountains filling the top. If the sky looks washed out, tap the stadium and slide it a touch darker.
card.best_time: There's no magic hour for the hillside, so go whenever you're passing by. At street level near the main gate and The MITT, game days get busy, so allow extra time for your photo.
card.selfie_here: Head to the corner of Edgar and Dave outside the main gate, on the plaza beside the Griffey statue. Fans often stop here for photos, and the Mariners' operations chief calls it one of the best selfie areas outside the park. Use the front camera, hold it a little higher than your face, and zoom 0.5x if you want to squeeze in more of the scene.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back from The MITT, the giant bronze baseball mitt at the left field gate, while you pose next to it.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are not allowed inside the ballpark, and personal photos and video are fine if they're for your own use. It's unclear whether the stick ban applies outside the gates, so go stick-free. The best views from inside need a ticket, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Take two shots from the hill, one wide and one zoomed, then see which one you'd actually put on the fridge.
card.good_to_know: T-Mobile Park is home to the Seattle Mariners, with a retractable roof and room for 47,368 fans. The first game here was played on 15 July 1999. It was called Safeco Field until 1 January 2019.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Dr. Jose Rizal Park, on the Beacon Hill hillside east of the stadium, and face the ballpark so you're looking down over it. The map will route you there, and the Navigate buttons take you to the subject.

card.hook: Picture a row of strangers shoulder to shoulder at a railing, all pointing their phones at the same Space Needle, and nobody minding a bit. That's Kerry Park at sunset, and you're about to join in.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, along the railing in Kerry Park on West Highland Drive, and face south. Downtown Seattle and the Space Needle fill the view in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the full skyline. Drop to 0.5x if you want the sculpture and the city in one shot, then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the Space Needle or Mount Rainier.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the skyline, then drag the brightness slider down a little (darker) so the sky keeps its colour and the buildings don't wash out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon to sunset usually suits this south-facing view, but it's busier then, so be patient and wait for a gap at the railing. Clear days are your best bet for spotting Mount Rainier.
card.selfie_here: Try the railing at the west (far) end of the park, where the view is least blocked, so the skyline and Space Needle stay clear behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and hold your phone a bit high with the city over your shoulder. The low wall near the middle is where most people pose, so it's a dependable backdrop, just expect company.
card.rules_and_safety: Guides suggest leaving bulky gear at home because it blocks the railing; that's advice, not a posted park rule. One visitor reported part of the lower area closed for tree pruning, so check conditions before you go.
card.challenge: Walk up to the hollow Changing Form sculpture and frame the Space Needle through it, like a picture inside a picture.
card.good_to_know: Albert and Katharine Kerry, who lived nearby, gave this 1.26-acre park to the city in 1927 so anyone who stopped here could enjoy the view. The steel sculpture in the middle, Changing Form, is 15 feet (4.6 m) tall and was installed in 1971. For a fuller skyline with less shrubbery and no railing in the picture, walk a short way to the right to the dirt mound.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, along the railing in Kerry Park on West Highland Drive, and face south. Downtown Seattle and the Space Needle fill the view in front of you.

card.hook: Picture a stack of glass boxes wrapped in a giant steel net, sitting between ordinary downtown buildings. That's the Seattle Central Library, and it looks like nothing else on the street.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of 4th Avenue and Spring Street and face east. From here the middle of the building is to the east, about 1 minute on foot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a head-on shot of the diamond grid. If the whole tower won't fit from the pavement, tap 0.5x. To fill the screen with the pattern, try 2x or 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the building's edges, and hold your phone upright so the sides don't lean in.
card.best_time: Go between 9 and 11 am or at dusk, which a travel guide recommends for the best light here. At dusk, switch on night mode and rest your phone against a wall or post to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the sidewalk across from the main entrance steps, or the 4th Avenue and Spring Street corner. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the glass facade behind you, so the diamond grid fills the background.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the plaza by the red LIBRARY sign, so they can frame you with the whole building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Staff may ask you to stop if you use flash inside, so skip it. One guide suggests a selfie from the highest viewing point only if you're not scared of heights.
card.challenge: Find a spot where the diamond grid fills your whole screen, then see if you can take the shot without the sides leaning.
card.good_to_know: The library opened on 23 May 2004 and is 11 storeys, about 57 metres (185 feet) tall. It was designed by Rem Koolhaas and Joshua Prince-Ramus of OMA, with Seattle firm LMN Architects. It has nearly 10,000 custom-sized windows, and it's the third library on this block.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of 4th Avenue and Spring Street and face east. From here the middle of the building is to the east, about 1 minute on foot.

selfie_spots.why: The guide lists this as a spot that shows the building's soaring lines, and it gives the frame behind you the most building surface.

card.hook: Rusty old gas-plant towers on one side, the Space Needle and downtown glittering across the water on the other. Seattle doesn't serve up this mix of old industry and city skyline many other places.
card.stand_here: Stand at the top of the grassy hill (Kite Hill) in Gas Works Park and face south across Lake Union toward downtown. Guides disagree on the best spot on the hilltop, so stroll around the lawn a little before you settle.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole skyline across the lake. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the Space Needle and towers closer, then 0.5x for the rusty structures up close.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line, then let the rusty structures fill one side of the frame with the skyline on the other.
card.best_time: Sunset and blue hour are the favourites, when the sky colours up and the city lights start to come on. Parking lots near Northlake Way fill quickly on summer evenings, so allow extra time.
card.selfie_here: Try beside the sundial at the top of Kite Hill, a popular photo spot with the park's widest views of the lake and downtown. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and check on screen that the skyline or the old plant is peeking over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the foot of the long brick staircase on the west side of the old plant while you climb or stand on the stairs, so the plant and skyline fit behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep to the public paths, because some of the rusty structures are fenced off, and don't climb the towers. The lake water is contaminated, so stay out of it. Events or fireworks can close parts of the park, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a frame where the sundial sits at the bottom, the Space Needle sits on the horizon, and a rusty tower sneaks in at the side. That's three things in one shot!
card.good_to_know: Gas Works Park covers 19.1 acres and is built around a coal gasification plant that ran from 1906 to 1956. Seattle bought the site in 1962 and the park opened in 1975, designed by Richard Haag. It's the only surviving plant of its kind in the United States, and some of the old machinery has been painted and reused in the children's play barn.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the top of the grassy hill (Kite Hill) in Gas Works Park and face south across Lake Union toward downtown. Guides disagree on the best spot on the hilltop, so stroll around the lawn a little before you settle.

card.hook: Picture the Space Needle sitting inside a giant dark doughnut. That's the Volunteer Park shot, and yes, locals really do call the sculpture "The Doughnut".
card.stand_here: Head for Isamu Noguchi's Black Sun sculpture, across from the Seattle Asian Art Museum, and stand right at it. Face the sculpture and look through its round hole to find the Space Needle.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to see how the Needle sits in the hole, then try 2x to bring it closer and fill more of the ring. Save zoom 0.5x for the museum or the wide lawns.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the Space Needle, then slide the brightness down a touch to make it a bit darker, so the sky stays blue and the sculpture doesn't wash out the picture.
card.best_time: Guides recommend morning. Check the light on the day, because haze can hide the Needle.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the lawn or path in front of the Volunteer Park Conservatory (1400 E Galer St) with the glasshouse behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to fit the symmetrical glass front over your shoulder, and hold the phone a little higher than your face.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the circular drive off the park's main entrance at 14th Ave East and East Prospect Street, and ask a passer-by to frame you with the whole water tower behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos are generally welcome, but commercial photography or drones may need permits. The conservatory doesn't allow professional photography. If you pose on the water tower's steps, take care, as they may be wet and slippery.
card.challenge: Take three shots, each one small step sideways from the last, and pick the one where the Needle sits dead centre in the ring.
card.good_to_know: The city bought the land in 1876, and the Olmsted Brothers were brought in to design the park in 1903. The brick water tower dates from 1906 and the glass conservatory from 1912. The Art Deco museum opened in 1932 as the original Seattle Art Museum.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Isamu Noguchi's Black Sun sculpture, across from the Seattle Asian Art Museum, and stand right at it. Face the sculpture and look through its round hole to find the Space Needle.

card.hook: Picture a 53-metre circle hanging out over the water, with the whole downtown skyline lined up behind it like it booked the spot. That's the Seattle Great Wheel, and it makes it very easy to look like you know what you're doing.
card.stand_here: Head to Pier 57, right at the end of the pier where the wheel stands. Face the wheel so the downtown skyline and Elliott Bay sit behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the wheel with the skyline and bay behind it. If you're close and the whole wheel won't fit, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the gondolas or the skyline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the wheel on one side of the frame and let the skyline and water fill the rest, then hold your phone level so the wheel stays round.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk is lovely, because the wheel's lights show up against the sky and the bay. Hours can change, so check the schedule on the day.
card.selfie_here: Try the wooden decking at the base of the wheel at Miner's Landing on Pier 57, with the wheel behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you want the whole circle over your shoulder, and let the planks lead the eye. Another option is the Bell Street walking bridge, facing back toward the wheel, but check the spot first as it's a photo-guide pick.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Pier 66 waterfront, far enough back to fit the full wheel and downtown in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photography is generally allowed at Miner's Landing Pier 57, but professional photography or filming may need permits from management. Skip shooting through the gondola windows, because glass reflections spoil the picture.
card.challenge: Get the wheel perfectly round in your frame, with the horizon dead straight and a very smug look on your face.
card.good_to_know: The Great Wheel opened in June 2012 and was then the tallest Ferris wheel on the West Coast. It's the only wheel of its design in North America built out over water, reaching about 12 metres beyond the pier's edge. Its 42 enclosed gondolas take riders around three turns in about 12 minutes.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Pier 57, right at the end of the pier where the wheel stands. Face the wheel so the downtown skyline and Elliott Bay sit behind it.

card.hook: Imagine a bold orange-red steel giant with the Space Needle sitting in the gap beside it, like it was placed there on purpose. That's the Eagle view at Olympic Sculpture Park, and it's a good one.
card.stand_here: Walk into the park to Alexander Calder's Eagle, the big orange-red sculpture, and go round to its west side. Face the Space Needle, with Eagle's steel in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so Eagle and the Space Needle both fit in the frame. Switch to 1x for Echo, the tall white head, with the Sound and sky behind it. For close-up abstract shots of Wake's steel walls, try 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the Space Needle or the sky, then slide it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour and Eagle doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Evening is the winner, around golden hour and sunset, when the colours warm up and the steel stands out against the sky. At sunset, check that the Space Needle hasn't turned into a silhouette you didn't want.
card.selfie_here: Stand beneath Calder's Eagle, between its legs, with the Space Needle behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep your hands off the steel. For a second backdrop, try the Louise Bourgeois 'Father and Son' fountain on the southwest corner at waterfront level, where a forum visitor describes the Space Needle in the background.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the west side of Eagle and shoot at 0.5x or 1x, so the sculpture and the Space Needle frame you.
card.rules_and_safety: The museum has a no-touch policy, so don't climb on or lean against the artworks. If you wander down to the waterfront beach, watch the tides and wear sensible shoes. Check the official site for opening times, closures and any rules on commercial photography.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, crouch low and tilt your phone up until Eagle's red steel slices right into the sky. Bonus points if the Space Needle pops up in the gap.
card.good_to_know: Olympic Sculpture Park is a free outdoor park run by the Seattle Art Museum. It sits on a 9-acre site beside Puget Sound that used to be industrial, and it opened on 20 January 2007. Eagle dates from 1971, and its paint was fully renewed in 2020, so it should look crisp.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk into the park to Alexander Calder's Eagle, the big orange-red sculpture, and go round to its west side. Face the Space Needle, with Eagle's steel in front of you.

card.hook: Somebody's California road trip ended badly: a huge concrete troll has grabbed their Volkswagen Beetle right off the bridge above. It's the only photo stop in Seattle where the car is part of the sculpture.
card.stand_here: Stand in Troll Knoll Forest, the little garden park right beside the troll. The troll is just to the south-west of you, so face south-west.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the troll and the garden greenery into one frame. Tap 2x for a tighter shot of the face and the Beetle, or go to 0.5x if you move closer and want the bridge overhead too.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the troll's head and hand on one of the lines, with a few plants in the foreground; if the bright sky washes out the concrete, tap the troll's face and make it a little darker.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, ideally on a weekday or early in the day. Weekends can get crowded and you may wait for a clear frame.
card.selfie_here: Climb the short stairway up the troll and stand behind its head, or pose in the palm or beside the Beetle. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and let the troll and the bridge fill in behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across Troll Avenue N, on the far side of the street north of the barricades, and shoot wide so the bridge is in, while you pose by the troll.
card.rules_and_safety: You're under a busy bridge, so keep out of the traffic lanes and watch for no-parking signs if you drive. Climbing is flagged as risky on some pages, so follow any signs on site and use your own judgement. The stairs are reported as fairly new, so check they're open.
card.challenge: Can you get the hubcap eye, the shaggy hair and the Beetle all in one shot, with you grinning in the corner?
card.good_to_know: Four artists made the Fremont Troll in 1990, inspired by Scandinavian folklore about trolls living under bridges. It stands 18 ft (5.5 m) high and is made of steel rebar, wire and concrete. The Beetle in its hand is a real one with a California licence plate.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Troll Knoll Forest, the little garden park right beside the troll. The troll is just to the south-west of you, so face south-west.

card.hook: Look for the pointy pyramid hat on the Seattle skyline. That's Smith Tower, and it might be the easiest building in town to pick out in a photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in Occidental Square, a short walk to the south-west of the tower in Pioneer Square, and face the tower so its pyramid crown rises over the old streets with the square's green space in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the crown, the buildings and the green space in one frame, or try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for just the pyramid top. Save 0.5x for Yesler Way or for when you walk close to the base.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower's brightest face, then slide it a little darker so the sky stays blue and the pale crown keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Golden hour is best, when the low, warm light falls on the tower and the old brick streets. If it has just rained, Yesler Way gives you reflections in the wet pavement.
card.selfie_here: Stand where James Street and Yesler Way meet, switch to the front camera and tilt it up so the tower rises above the parking garage over your shoulder. If your front camera has a 0.5x option, it will fit more of the scene in.
card.ask_someone: Stand on Yesler Way below 2nd Avenue and ask a passer-by to walk up and down the street until the whole tower fits in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The observation deck is a paid attraction, so check the official site if you want to go up. If you're planning a full photo shoot inside the building, get approval first.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the tower's crown sits in the top third and a tree frames the side, then try to keep the tower's edges perfectly straight. Bonus points if nobody walks through it.
card.good_to_know: Smith Tower was completed in 1914 at 38 storeys and 462 ft (141 m), among the tallest skyscrapers outside New York City at the time. It was the tallest building west of the Mississippi River until 1931, and the tallest on the US West Coast until the Space Needle overtook it in 1962. It's named after Lyman Cornelius Smith, the firearm and typewriter businessman who started the project, and became a Seattle landmark in 1984.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Occidental Square, a short walk to the south-west of the tower in Pioneer Square, and face the tower so its pyramid crown rises over the old streets with the square's green space in front of you.

card.hook: From Jose Rizal Bridge, Seattle's tallest building isn't a big close-up, it's one tall shape in a crowd of downtown offices. Your game here is simple: find the tallest one and pick it out.
card.stand_here: Stand on Jose Rizal Bridge and face north-west, looking across the city. Walk along the bridge until nothing blocks your view of the towers, then look for Columbia Center as the tallest one.
card.zoom: Zoom 1x will make the tower look small and lost among its neighbours, so try zoom 2x to 5x, depending on your phone. Only use zoom 0.5x if you want the bridge and sky in the picture too.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then slide it a little darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the towers. At dusk, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to keep the phone steady while the city lights come on.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and zoom 0.5x so you fit in the frame, with the skyline over your shoulder. Don't expect the tower to be big behind you from this far away, so check the shot and move along the bridge if another building gets in the way.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines, keep the horizon level, and put Columbia Center slightly off-centre with a little sky above it. Can you get it to look like three towers standing side by side?
card.good_to_know: Columbia Center is the tallest building in Washington state: 76 storeys and 933 ft (284 m), finished in 1985. Its three tall faces curve inwards and step back twice, which is why it looks like three towers side by side. There's a public observatory on the 73rd floor, so check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Jose Rizal Bridge and face north-west, looking across the city. Walk along the bridge until nothing blocks your view of the towers, then look for Columbia Center as the tallest one.

selfie_research.notes: Weak evidence overall. No page I found names a spot where a visitor stands with Columbia Center directly behind them, and no page names a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole tower, so ask_someone_spot is null. The two selfie spots are only places where pages show the tower photographed; they are not confirmed selfie locations. The Sky View Observatory on the 73rd floor is the most-recommended photo spot, but it is the view from inside the tower, not a spot with the tower behind the visitor, so I left it out. A selfie-stick/tripod tip appears only for the Seattle Selfie Museum, not for Columbia Center, so I did not list it as a rule. No safety point is stated for this landmark.

card.hook: Picture a game day: a river of fans in team colours flowing towards the gates while giant arches rise over their heads. That's the shot, and it's free.
card.stand_here: Head to Muckleshoot Heritage Plaza on the north side of Lumen Field and face south. The arches rise overhead and the entrance sits right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the arches overhead and the crowd below. Then switch to 1x for a more natural look.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the arches up with the top third of the frame, with the crowd or entrance path in front for depth.
card.best_time: Game days are the liveliest, when the crowds stream towards the entrance. Crowds depend on events, so check the stadium's calendar before you go.
card.selfie_here: Stay in Muckleshoot Heritage Plaza on the north side, where a guide calls it the best pregame exterior spot. Use the front camera at 0.5x and stand so the arches are overhead and the crowd flows past behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are not permitted inside Lumen Field. Tickets are only needed for events inside, so the outside views cost nothing.
card.challenge: Catch the arches in the top third of your frame and a fan in team colours walking through the foreground. Bonus points if it looks like they're heading straight for you.
card.good_to_know: Lumen Field was built between 2000 and 2002 on the site of the old Kingdome. It holds 68,740 people for NFL games, so it's a lot to squeeze onto a phone screen. Seahawks fans also twice claimed the Guinness World Record for the loudest crowd roar at an outdoor stadium, in 2013 and 2014.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Muckleshoot Heritage Plaza on the north side of Lumen Field and face south. The arches rise overhead and the entrance sits right in front of you.

card.hook: Most people stroll right past this entrance, and that's the fun of it. A tall gate, a peek of green, and the sound of falling water in the middle of Pioneer Square.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Main Street and 2nd Avenue South, at the entrance gateway on the sidewalk, and face in through the tall gate. The garden and its waterfall are to the north-west, about 1 minute on foot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x at the gate so the frame and the green beyond sit nicely. Once you're inside, switch to zoom 0.5x to fit the waterfall and the buildings above it, then try zoom 2x or more (depends on your phone) to pick out the water or a plant.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the gate opening in the middle, and tap the green leaves, then slide to darker if the white water or sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Go in the daytime, when the garden is open. A bright overcast day or the morning keeps the shady garden and the sky from fighting each other.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the paved walkway in front of the 22-foot waterfall, with the tables or ornamental trees beside you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the falling water over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The park is privately owned but open to the public in the day and locked at night, so check the posted hours before you go. Small-scale photography needs no permission, but commercial shoots do. Keep to the paths and don't block other visitors. A security guard is on duty inside.
card.challenge: Take one photo through the gate that only shows green and a glimmer of water, then see if a friend can guess where it is.
card.good_to_know: Waterfall Garden Park was made in 1978 at the original United Parcel Service building. It's only about 18 by 24 metres, yet the man-made waterfall is 22 feet (6.7 m) tall. The Japanese-style garden around it won an environmental award in 1981.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Main Street and 2nd Avenue South, at the entrance gateway on the sidewalk, and face in through the tall gate. The garden and its waterfall are to the north-west, about 1 minute on foot.
